primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' -- an account of the January 1999 confrontation between pro- and anti-death penalty advocates, from the Court's temporary restraining order staying Leo Echegaray's execution to its lifting two weeks later, with CJP's own separate opinions reproduced.

A four-year statistical record of the Court's death penalty review showing that fewer than one third of the death sentences imposed by trial courts were affirmed, and the recurring grounds -- defective Informations, crimes not proven as charged, unproven aggravating circumstances and non-retroactivity -- on which penalties were reduced.

The jurisprudential development that the qualifying circumstances of the victim's minority and her relationship to the offender must both be alleged in the Information and proven, and CJP's conclusion that under this doctrine Echegaray himself should have received reclusion perpetua.

His standing constitutional thesis, set out in the Separate Opinion in People v. Echegaray reproduced in full: that the 1987 Constitution abolished rather than suspended the death penalty, and that RA 7659 failed the twin requirements of heinousness and compelling reasons.
The argument that capital punishment falls disproportionately on the poor, the powerless and the marginalized, and that its errors are irreversible once carried out.
sub_topics: CJP's admission that his prediction in Battles in the Supreme Court that death cases would occupy the Court's continuing attention had been too conservative, given the full-blown confrontation of January 1999.

The 8-5 Resolution of January 4, 1999 issuing a TRO good until June 15, 1999 on Atty. Te's motion, grounded on pending bills and a treaty said to be headed for ratification, holding that the merest chance that Congress might reconsider entitled Echegaray to a stay.

The furious reaction of nearly the entire officialdom, street rallies demanding the resignation or impeachment of the eight justices, and threats to individual magistrates, Court employees and their families -- including CJP's daughters, for whom he had to provide extra security.
The counterweight of support from Church and media groups, columnists, broadcasters and friends.

The President's declaration that he would veto any repeal or modification of RA 7659 and the House's Resolution No. 629 rejecting any review, which made it evident the law would not change before adjournment.

The Resolution of January 19, 1999 lifting the TRO, written by Justice Puno, answering the charge of overstepping: the Court changed not a comma of its decision, acted under its power to control the execution of its own judgments, and did not restrain the effectivity of a law.

Puno's further points that executive clemency does not deny courts control over the enforcement of their decisions, that a convict retains collateral rights, and that as life was at stake the Court refused to constitutionalize haste and the hysteria of some partisans.

CJP's short Separate Opinion reproduced in full: agreeing the Court had jurisdiction, accepting that the TRO should by its own terms be deemed lifted, but refusing to vote to lift it because that would enforce a law he considers unconstitutional, while deferring to the rule of law and the Court's contrary ruling.
Justice Vitug's parallel opinion on comity to a co-equal branch and his hope for a dispassionate congressional re-examination of the conditions sine qua non for imposing death.

The statistics from October 10, 1995 to October 10, 1999: 164 death cases reviewed, 53 affirmed covering 59 convicts, 74 reduced to reclusion perpetua, 12 reduced further, 9 remanded and 23 appellants acquitted.
The growth of the constitutional dissent from three justices in Echegaray to two and then to four in People v. Escala, and the standard clause thereafter reproduced in all death affirmations.

The four recurring grounds for reduction: insufficient allegations of heinousness in the Information; the crime charged not being the crime proven; failure to prove aggravating circumstances under Article 63; and crimes committed before RA 7659 took effect on December 31, 1993.
The doctrine that every element of the offense must be alleged so the accused can prepare his defense, applied to the seven new special circumstances that raise rape from reclusion perpetua to death.

The line of cases -- Perez, Dimapilis, Manggasin, Ponado, Larena, Puertollano -- reducing the penalty where minority or relationship was unalleged or where a claimed stepfather was in fact only the mother's common-law spouse.

The Romeo Gallo Resolution of September 29, 1999, where a final death judgment was reopened at the Public Attorney's Office's instance, with the Solicitor General joining the plea, and the penalty reduced.

CJP's contention that Echegaray's own Information alleged fatherhood that was never proven -- only that he was the confirmed lover of Rodessa's mother -- so his penalty should have been reduced, an error no jurisprudence can now undo.

The contrast between People v. Parazo, where a deaf-mute retardate tried without a sign language expert was granted a new trial, and People v. Esparas, where the Court by 11-3 refused to reopen the case of the first woman death convict; CJP voted with the minority of three to require the prosecution at least to comment.
His separate opinion in People v. Raquiño maintaining that reviewing and promulgating decisions for escaped death convicts unduly favors fugitives and encourages escape.

The hypothetical and real vote-splitting problem -- Dizon, Bantilan and Tapales -- in which differing appreciations of evidence combined with the four constitutional dissents could leave the death penalty short of a majority.

The reproduced Separate Opinion in People v. Echegaray: that Section 19 abolished the penalty prospectively and retroactively, so its restoration is an exception to be strictly construed and RA 7659 enjoys no presumption of constitutionality.

The heinousness argument: Congress never defined heinous, the preamble's epithets supply no workable standard, a preamble is not an integral part of a law, and RA 7659 merely reimposed death on crimes already so punishable.

The compelling reasons argument: Garcia's invocation of worsening peace and order and of justice, rebutted by Lagman's crime statistics and Lina's drug-arrest figures showing declines after 1987, and by the absence of empirical proof of deterrence.

The pro-life reading of the Constitution -- dignity, human rights, the ban on torture, protection of the unborn, rights to health, ecology and education -- and the primacy of the right to life over all other rights.

The Free Legal Assistance Group's profile of 165 death row convicts showing their poverty, occupations, languages and schooling, and CJP's answer to the objection that the law does not single out the poor.

The six-point epilogue on abolition, the new constitutional right against the death penalty, strict construction, the sanctity of every constitutional word, the twin congressional requirements, and the need to justify heinousness and compelling reasons crime by crime, closing with the Church's teaching in Evangelium Vitae.

stances.claim: RA 7659 is unconstitutional insofar as it prescribes the capital penalty, because the parts doing so fail the Constitution's requirements of heinousness and compelling reasons; RA 8177 falls with it, since it merely prescribes the manner of implementation.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-text argument: reading Section 19 as an abolition with both prospective and retroactive aspects, so that restoration is an exception strictly construed against the State

stances.claim: Even while holding the law unconstitutional, he defers to the rule of law and abides by the ruling of the majority that RA 7659 and RA 8177 are constitutional and that death may be imposed by lethal injection.
stances.rhetorical_move: dissent-with-submission: stating the objection in full and then expressly bowing to the institution's decision

stances.claim: Congress's stated compelling reasons -- worsening peace and order and justice -- were not compelling and were in fact non-existent, since police and Dangerous Drugs Board figures showed murder, robbery, homicide and drug arrests declining after the 1987 abolition.
stances.rhetorical_move: turning the sponsor's own statistics against him by quoting the Garcia-Lagman and Lina interpellations at length

stances.claim: The preamble of RA 7659 supplies no workable standard of heinousness; calling crimes grievous, odious and hateful is not a substitute for an objective juridical definition, and a preamble is not an integral part of a law.
stances.rhetorical_move: metaphorical dismissal -- blood called blue is still crimson, gumamela renamed rose grows no thorns -- backed by a rule of statutory construction

stances.claim: Under the Court's own strict readings of criminal Informations, Echegaray's penalty should have been reduced to reclusion perpetua, since the Information alleged a fatherhood that was never proven.
stances.rhetorical_move: applying the Court's later doctrine retrospectively to its own first affirmed death case, then noting the remedy is now impossible

stances.claim: The death penalty falls on the poor and powerless, who cannot afford the extensive preparation capital cases require -- as this very case showed, the constitutionality issue being raised only belatedly by free legal counsel.
stances.rhetorical_move: socio-economic profile as evidence, followed by anticipating and answering the objection that the law does not single out the poor

stances.claim: Reviewing and promulgating decisions in death cases while the appellant remains at large unduly favors fugitives, countenances a trifling with judicial processes and encourages escape.
stances.rhetorical_move: incentive analysis of a procedural rule, pressed in a separate opinion against the majority

notable_anecdotes: The month in which CJP was singled out for the most venal criticism because he had publicly opposed the capital penalty in Battles in the Supreme Court, and had to provide extra security for his daughters after they received hate calls and bodily threats.

The timing that forced the Court's hand: Echegaray was to be executed at 3:00 p.m. on the first working day after his motion was filed, which the Court cited as compelling extreme caution because all rights stop at the graveyard.
Justice Puno waxing poetic in the Resolution lifting the TRO, calling the courts a hatchery of justice whose flame cannot be ignited by the rage of the mob.
The internal friction in People v. Escala, where the repetitive dissent drew the ire of the majority and led to an agreed standard clause reproduced in all future death affirmations.
The reopening of Romeo Gallo's already final death judgment after the Public Attorney's Office pointed out the defect in the Information, with the Solicitor General joining the plea for reduction.

Josefina Esparas's account that she had not escaped but had visited her mother in Caloocan City under escort and waited in vain for the policeman who never returned, and CJP's vote with the minority of three to have the prosecution at least comment.

Marlon Parazo's case, in which a death sentence was set aside after medical examination showed him to be a deaf-mute retardate with a mental age of seven years and nine months tried without a sign language expert.
The remembered support of Church and media groups, columnists, broadcasters and friends during the weeks of lynch mobs and screaming headlines, whom CJP says the Court will never forget.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Leadership by Example: The Davide Standard' recounted the January 1999 confrontation over capital punishment. Justice Panganiban reported that the Court, voting 8-5 on January 4, issued a temporary restraining order hours before Leo Echegaray's scheduled execution, holding that the merest chance Congress might reconsider the Death Penalty Law entitled him to a stay, and that nearly the entire officialdom reacted furiously, with rallies demanding the eight justices' resignation and threats reaching magistrates, employees and families -- his own daughters requiring extra security because he had publicly opposed the penalty in his earlier book. After the President vowed to veto any repeal and the House passed Resolution No. 629 rejecting review, the Court lifted the order on January 19 in a Resolution by Justice Puno, which insisted the Court had changed not a comma of its decision, had exercised only its power to control the execution of its own judgments, and had refused to constitutionalize haste because all rights stop at the graveyard. CJP reproduced his own short opinion refusing to vote for lifting, since that would enforce a law he considers unconstitutional, while deferring to the rule of law. He then set out four years of statistics -- 164 death cases reviewed, 53 affirmed, 74 reduced to reclusion perpetua, 12 reduced further, 9 remanded, 23 acquittals -- and catalogued the grounds for reduction, chiefly the failure to allege in the Information both the victim's minority and her relationship to the offender, illustrated through Perez, Dimapilis, Manggasin, Ponado, Larena, Puertollano and the reopened Gallo case. Applying that doctrine, he argued Echegaray himself should have received reclusion perpetua, an error no jurisprudence could now undo. He discussed Parazo, the refusal to reopen Esparas, his objection to reviewing appeals of escaped convicts, and the vote-splitting that could leave death short of a majority. The chapter closed with his Separate Opinion in Echegaray reproduced in full, arguing that the 1987 Constitution abolished the penalty, that RA 7659 defined neither heinousness nor compelling reasons, that crime statistics contradicted its premises, and that the law fell on the poor and had no place in the legal firmament.
